Under all kritik. Bedrövlig på alla vis. Förfärlig, pretentiös och trångsynt—allt på samma gång. Det här är dålig fringe indie konst at its finest, tondöv inför allt den försöker röra och göra, som för närmast utomjordliga orsaker upphöjs till något coolt eller bra eller edgy??—när det sista den borde förknippas med är priser och mainstream. Det här är en spegelbild på hur djupt vi låtit gräva oss ifrån vad som en gång kunde kallas kvalitet. Alla som jobbat med denna film på nåt vis borde skämmas, alla som belönat detta borde skämmas ännu mer. Inte ens coola musik/dans-nummer, som ju bör vara denna karnevals saving grace, klarar den av. Eftersom Ryan Coogler är så inkompetent på att viska symboltongue och sälja sin ormolja, kommer jag symboliskt skänka honom en halv stjärna. En halv stjärna som ingen förtjänar, men som man antagligen bär med heder i denna uppochnedvända cirkusvärld. Jag är ju de facto clownen som faktiskt satt och såg genom 138 minuter av detta brinnkära helvete. 🤡

Un des pires films que j’ai vus de ma vie. J’aimerais exagérer mais ce n’est pas le cas. Je pensais lui rentrer dedans pour des raisons qui me sont propres mais j’ai tout d’abord était surpris puis dévasté par la nullité de ce tâcheron de Coogler. Photographie immonde, le chef opérateur complètement éclaté qui nous a offert le premier film IMAX qui ressemble à une vidéo d’Iphone Pro Max. Une écriture pitoyable, grossièrement démonstrative, un Jordan qui surjoue pour tenir sa double face, surtout celle de Smoke… Des discussions qui n’ont aucun sens à certains moments… Profondément ridicule… Même pas risible, ridicule. Quand on a sa famille à la production, effectivement les garde-fous n’existent pas… La roue libre est totale. la nullité abyssale… Je passe sur la gratuité de la scène Django, tellement gratuite dans le scénario qu’elle peut naître que d’un cerveau malade assoiffé d’apaisement. Peele est néfaste, Coogler n’est qu’une tache. J’arrête là, tant la liste peut être longue et je ne veux pas subir BLM dont la sensibilité paraît à fleur de peau. Je sauve la musique… entachée d’une moquerie envers les blancs en les faisant passer pour les consanguins de Délivrance… Le film fait plus pitié qu’autre chose. One of the worst movies I’ve ever seen. I wish I were exaggerating, but I’m not. I went in ready to tear it apart for my own reasons, but I was first surprised and then devastated by the sheer incompetence of that hack, Coogler. Hideous cinematography—the DP was a total disaster, giving us the first IMAX movie that looks like an iPhone Pro Max video. Pitiful, heavy-handed writing; Jordan overacting to pull off his dual persona—especially the "Smoke" side... Conversations that make absolutely no sense at times... Deeply ridiculous... Not even "so bad it's funny," just ridiculous. When you have family producing the film, there are obviously no safeguards... It’s completely off the rails. Abysmal quality... I won't even get into the gratuitous *Django* scene—so gratuitous it could only have sprung from a sick mind desperate for some kind of catharsis. Peele is toxic; Coogler is nothing but a stain. I’ll stop there—the list could go on forever, and I don’t want to deal with the BLM crowd, who seem to have such thin skin. The only saving grace is the music... though even that is marred by mocking white people, portraying them as the inbreds from *Deliverance*... The film is just pathetic, more than anything else.

Urgh, another bit of very popular media that makes me feel like I am from a different planet. It reaches for everything and achieves nothing. What is this film even meant to be? Is it meant to be social commentary? It is about social history but I don't know what the commentary is, other than maybe don't trust the KKK? Is it supposed to be a slow-burn Southern Gothic film? I mean, it is slow. The first half is littered with scenes that work the same way, recruiting a new party member, and we learn nothing new. 10mins in we know the two main characters are (1) brothers, (2) naughty, and (3) the brothers did naughty things in Chicago and now they're back home. And the film refuses to give us anything more. And the Chicago thing never gets paid off. Neither does the Native American stuff, or the KKK stuff, other than the shootout that feels so detached from the rest of the film it may as well have been a deleted scene. Is it meant to be a post-modern genre piece? The film plays with film form a bit (changes in aspect ratio, that one time travel music montage, the long post credits sequence) - but to what end? They may as well have made every third scene play out in black and white, it would be just as "interesting" and nonsensical as what they did do. Is it just a fun horror romp with a twist? If so, what was that first hour all about? Just watch From Dusk Til Dawn, or Shaun of the Dead, or Suspiria or something. And even the Oscar-winning best parts of the film fell flat for me. Michael B Jordon plays two versions of the same character, except one wears a blue hat and the other wears a red hat. The music is okay at times but laughably bad at others - with the ultra intense electric guitar licks sounding like something straight out of Lethal Weapon. And I get it - it's hard for a film to live up to the hype. But I saw Obsession way after the hype and I loved that film

As the last sane critic on Earth, I feel honor-bound to address the Best Original Screenplay nomination for Sinners. It would be natural for you to assume that the nomination of a script so ill conceived, poorly thought-out, and badly written would cause me a considerable amount of distress. Fortunately, you would be mistaken. The idea that Ryan Coogler, writer of Fruitvale Station, Creed, and Black Panther, thought the screenplay for Sinners was good enough to shoot is so absurd that I can only conclude that the creation of Sinners — from conception to reception — is a piece of performance art. I therefore applaud the nomination as a vital component of the work.1 To spend $90M shooting your shitty first draft and have the result be gobs of money and maximum acclaim is a note-perfect enactment of the classic fable The Emperor’s New Clothes. That the emperor is a truly talented and undeniably successful Black filmmaker weaving his own “magic” clothes adds a topical and challenging dimension to the piece. The idea that Coogler wrongly believes Sinners has a cogent, completed script does not bear discussion. You might as well point out that Coogler had co-writers for both Creed and Black Panther and that the solo-authored Fruitvale Station is several orders of magnitude less ambitious. I will not have it! The very suggestion that Ryan Coogler was maybe never a great writer or thinker in the first place is off the table, regardless of how strongly a literary analysis of Sinners supports that conclusion. You can’t have The Emperor’s New Clothes if the emperor is wearing anything at all. It doesn’t work if his garments are merely simple or unattractive. He has to be full-on butt-naked. For the performance piece to work, the script for Sinners cannot be merely bad. It must be bereft of any cogent meaning, terrible to the point of semantic and thematic incoherence. In this, Coogler has achieved his aim. Find out how: lastsanecritic.substack.com/p/the-script-for-sinners-is-so-bad

• This film was a major disappointment to me. There were three dimensions where I think it had to succeed. First, the period piece about African Americans in the Jim Crow south, second, the horror or monster movie, and third, the interplay between these two themes. Unfortunately I don’t think it did well enough on any of these dimensions. • The twins are not interesting characters to me, they are caricatured as exceptionally masculine, aggressive, and competent. • The action sequences were boring and the special effects relating to the vampires and violence were inconsistent, which was distracting. • The scene where Sammy performs in the clubhouse and brings forth music from all times, past and future, is quite powerful and well done. • In my opinion, there should have been more subtlety in the way race was handled in the film. The white people are the monsters, they have corny music, and they turn out to be Klan associates. Once converted, they offer the remaining black people the chance to live forever, as a single (race-blind) community, but they have to forfeit their souls to do so. • I didn’t like the writing, which further detracted from my experience

This film did not know what it was doing. It had great music, cinematography, characters, and what looked to be a great plot. Unfortunately this great plot was never flourished out. 2 and a half hours should be more than enough time to make a great film with so many cool elements that Sinners tried to include, however the movie started off slow not knowing much of what it was actually getting at. Even after the vampires came into the plot, the film did not pick up, as the vibes immediately changed. It was very confusing what to focus at: vampires? Or past, present, and future musical connections? I personally was a big fan of the music, yet the film actually did nothing with it besides showing that the vampires sing. It felt like a must to have more music and they just skipped over that. On top of that there is no explanation for the vampires and their motives, making me not actually care for them as characters I could truly understand. I am happy though they had some vampire elements that are less common in modern media such as asking permission to come in. While I’m being negative here the film is saved by the performances of the actors, the musical scenes, and the film’s breathtaking cinematography. Stand out performance for Micheal B. Jordan. In summary, this film focuses too much on getting to know the main characters, just to immediately skip to a climax with little if not any build up. For a movie so hyped up and talked about I expected so much more. Don’t even get me started on the useless scene of killing those racist men at the end. Aye yi yi.

Shallow Depth of Field, Soft Focus and Anomorphic Blur. The actual Hollywood cultural zietgeist. The modern fad of movies today is new filmmakers and directors trying to inject their films with that enigmatic juice that makes something cinema, that unexplainable feeling of the movies, ironic as most of these new directors are doing everything but making their films feel like cinema. The biggest victim of this new ideology is the visual department, most films are entirley filmed in shallow depth of field, which to put it simply is enhancing a subject and basically leaving the entire background out of focus and blurry (anomorphic blur) this is also called soft focus, when only the subject is in focus. Before today where its now considered normal to shoot 80% of your film in soft focus, movies used alot more deep focus, where subjects are crisp but the backgrounds where enriched with detail, visible detail and not indescrible blurry backgrounds. Now there are positives to using soft focus, it's not like a new technique that suddenly has been founded, filmmakers have always used soft focus, but in moderation, restricting to key character moments when all that is important in a scene is the character. Nowdays soft focus is used to film every scene, it removes world building and the distinct personality of the film. And it's not always a filmmaker problem, this issue has stemmed from studios becoming too lazy to fund and budget set designs properly, and will encourage shallow focus to paste over the cracks of the image being built and spin it as a "cinematic" effect. It's one of the worst trends in todays industry. Sinners is far from the only movie that falls victim to this terrible trend, but it is by far one of the most notable and consequential. 16 academy award nominations were granted to this movie, that is the MOST ever, what does that tell studios and aspiring filmmakers? that movies should be like this? that is a very dangerous precedent to set. ‘Sinners’ got a lot of hype and everybody was posting it to their Letterboxd Last Four, so I thought there must be something more to it. However, turns out it was a bit overhyped—certainly not worthy of 18 Oscar nominations. It’s basically a big-budget horror film with some not-so-subtle metaphors for cultural and human exploitation. I certainly appreciate the intent of the film to reach a mainstream audience with a political message delivered by way of an allegory. Unfortunately, it’s not a particularly clever plot or a smart script. There are moments of artistry—the blending of multiple anachronistic musical genres into one scene, for example—but all that smarts gets overtaken by the conventional horror story plot points. My first complaint is, everything feels phony. The period wardrobes feel too new and perfect. The art direction looks too theme park. There are backdrops that are obviously CG. Compare the look of this film to ‘Hamnet’ or ‘Days of Heaven’, and you’ll know what I mean. The past was dirty and messy. Then there’s the camerawork. I keep saying this, but beautiful photography and precise movement isn’t everything. The camera should tell the story without drawing attention to itself. I felt like I was always noticing the camera’s movements instead of following the characters. Most disappointing was the script, which not only spells out the metaphor—in case you didn’t get it—but it also reduces the characters to stereotype gangster tough guys and any true relationships to either sex or violence. That’s just not reality. There’s also the lack of logic. How would people in the ‘20’s before the 100 years of popular vampire films all inherently know all the methods of dispensing with vampires? They exist during the say but burn up when exposed to sunlight? It’s okay if you don’t think about it, I guess. I’m rating it a 6 because it’s decently produced and semi-entertaining, but man, the insight and the poignancy were lost in the traditional horror and gore.

i finally got to watch this and I have such mixed feelings about this movie because it starts off amazing but ends up feeling pretty average the best part of the movie is definitely the beginning, i was completely mesmerized by the first hour of sinners, the way it honors 1930s black culture through its phenomenal music, vibrant lighting, and lived-in community spaces is genuinely breathtaking. everything from the old-school blues music to the way people dress and talk feels totally real, you get a great sense of how close the community is, and the movie takes its time showing you their daily lives, the lighting is  also super warm and pretty, and it just feels like a really cool, special historical movie that you haven't seen before. it built up this amazing world, and I was so excited to see where it was going. then the monsters show up and the movie immediately goes downhill, the second half completely forgets about the culture and the story it was building and it just turns into a brainless, generic monster movie. it’s literally just a checklist of boring horror tropes: monsters jumping out of closets, loud noises to startle you, and endless fighting where you can barely see what's happening, even having michael b. jordan play twins felt like a wasted gimmick because the movie becomes too basic to care i didn't hate it, and the first half is honestly worth the price of admission alone, I just wish the ending was as creative and unique as the beginning

"Raíces, blues y colmillos" Sinners es mucho más que una película de vampiros. Es un viaje al pasado para reivindicar la preservación de las culturas negras y minorías segregadas, su espiritualismo y esas raíces que la historia ha intentado arrancar. Y lo hace sin renunciar al entretenimiento: balazos, buena música y una acción que bebe de clásicos como Blade. La escenografía es un personaje más: el espacio se puede oler entre el sudor, la transpiración y la bebida. Ese filtro entre lo antiguo y lo nuevo funciona de maravilla. El final es satisfactorio y redentor, y te deja con el mensaje principal bien grabado: respetar siempre de dónde venimos. No todo es perfecto: los efectos cumplen (prostéticos y CGI), pero a veces flaquean, y los vampiros pierden poder en ciertos momentos, haciendo que la pelea contra la horda se sienta lenta e inverosímil. Aun así, la experiencia vale la pena.

Ryan Coogler swinging for the fences and connecting almost every time. The first hour is pure hangout-movie pleasure — building this world, this juke joint, these characters — and then it just detonates once Remmick shows up and the vampire mythology kicks in. That music sequence where Sammie plays and the film bends time to show every era of Black music converging in one room is one of the most audacious, purely cinematic things I've seen in a theater in years. Ludwig Göransson's score is doing insane amounts of heavy lifting throughout. Michael B. Jordan pulling off two fully distinct performances as Smoke and Stack without it ever feeling like a gimmick, and the way the film uses vampirism as a metaphor for cultural theft never feels heavy-handed — it earns every beat. If anything holds it back from a full five it's that the back half's genre turn moves so fast some of the character work from the first hour doesn't fully pay off the way I wanted. Still, this is a filmmaker operating at the absolute top of his craft. Original, ambitious, and unlike anything else that came out last year.
